title: Cross-model KV adapter, lazy dematerialization, and kernel polymorphism for paged attention
creator: Amelia Park
description: Problem: As we support mixed-model fleets and quantization variants, KV slots are duplicated or pinned to incompatible kernel paths which increases GPU residency and causes tail-latency spikes during decode/prefill. Goal: introduce a lightweight cross-model KV adapter layer that enables stored KV fragments to be represented in a compact, model-agnostic form and to be lazily dematerialized off the hot GPU heap. At decode/prefill time the runtime will select a polymorphic kernel path that either uses an upcasted compact fragment or triggers an on-demand rehydration. This ticket implements the adapter and scheduler changes to reduce per-tenant GPU footprint while preserving tail-latency SLOs.
technical_approach: 1) KV fragment canonicalization: define a compact on-disk/inert representation for KV fragments (quantized tensors + metadata) with a small header containing model-variant compatibility hints and a residency score. 2) Lazy dematerialization pipeline: background worker moves low-residency fragments to compressed GPU-host pinned pages or NVMe cache and marks slot as dematerialized. 3) Polymorphic kernel selector: extend kernel selector to accept compacted fragments and select either a direct compact-kernel path or a rehydrate-and-run path based on predicted restore cost vs SLO budget. 4) Predictive prefill advisory: integrate a tiny bloom filter index that tracks recent token spans and guides prefill scheduler to rehydrate only likely-needed fragments ahead of time (soft-handoff). 5) Admission & backpressure: admission controller uses per-request urgency and measured restore latency distribution to decide whether to inline restore, queue the request, or route to fallback model variant.
decision_log: 2025-02-19: Chosen 'compact canonicalization' format over full tensor consolidation to minimize restore CPU work (decision by runtime team).
2025-02-22: Agreed to implement bloom-filter guided predictive rehydrate instead of full ML predictor for initial rollout to limit complexity.
2025-02-26: Opted for a generic adapter layer (cross-model) rather than model-specific shims to support future open-model onboarding.
2025-03-03: Deferred hardware-tier NVMe direct-mapped restore for later cycle due to driver cert time; using host pinned pages for now.
acceptance_criteria: Mean GPU active KV footprint reduced by >=18% for mixed-variant benchmark workload (Mix-A) during steady-state.
95th percentile decode latency for tail-heavy workload does not regress by more than 5ms vs baseline with identical SLOs.
Canary deployment for 10% traffic for dedicated customers shows no more than 0.5% increase in error rate and acceptable cost savings.
Automated unit and integration tests that simulate dematerialize/rehydrate cycles with synthetic prefill patterns included in CI.
Monitoring dashboards created with residency, restore-latency-percentiles, bloom-index hit rate, and kernel-path distribution.
Security review completed for moving customer-derived KV fragments to host persistence cache and documented in security ticket.
test_plan: Unit tests for canonicalization and header compatibility checks across model variants.
Microbench harness: simulate 100k slot dematerialize/rehydrate cycles, measure restore latency and CPU overlap.
End-to-end perf test: Mix-A workload (50% long-span chat + 50% short queries) run on staging with and without adapter; collect percentiles and GPU memory metrics.
Chaos test: force background worker pauses and validate request-level fallbacks and no customer-visible corruption.
Canary tests on dedicated cluster: 2-hour ramp, 10% traffic, monitor SLA and alerting thresholds.
rollout_plan: Roll out to internal staging first, run Mix-A benchmark and validate acceptance criteria.
Canary 1: 5% of host pools for non-critical tenants for 24h.
Canary 2: 10% dedicated pools for customers with low latency sensitivity for 48h.
Full rollout conditional on no regressions and successful security review.
risks_mitigation: Risk: Rehydrate latency could cause tail spikes. Mitigation: conservative admission controller that routes to fallback model variant when predicted restore exceeds per-request slack.
Risk: Incorrect canonicalization could corrupt outputs between model variants. Mitigation: compatibility checksum and strict fail-open tests that fallback to native slot when mismatch detected.
Risk: Extra CPU load from compression codecs. Mitigation: use lightweight per-fragment codec (FP16 pack + delta compression) and cap background worker concurrency by tenant weight.
Risk: Security/regulatory concerns for persisted fragments. Mitigation: encrypt fragments at rest with customer KMS keys when in private deployments and log access in audit trail.
Risk: Increased scheduler complexity. Mitigation: isolate algorithm behind adapter API and provide feature flag to revert to legacy behavior.
updates: 2025-02-19: Prototype canonicalizer implemented; initial unit tests added. Noted ~22% reduction in synthetic slot size for Mix-A sample set.
2025-02-24: Bloom-filter index prototype integrated with prefill advisor; initial false-positive rate ~0.8% at 1% memory overhead.
2025-02-28: Benchmarked polymorphic kernel selector with two kernel paths (compact vs restore); restore path median 12ms but 99th at 140ms before admission tuning.
2025-03-03: Admission controller added heuristics for urgency buckets; 99th restore latency reduced to 62ms under low-concurrency scenarios.
2025-03-05: Security review kickoff with Leila Ahmed; identified data-at-rest encryption requirement for private deployments.
notes: This ticket intentionally avoids a full ML predictor for rehydrate prediction to reduce rollout risk; follow-up ticket will evaluate ML-based predictors if bloom-filter approach shows limits.
We should coordinate with Dedicated ops to instrument tenant-weighted background worker limits to avoid noisy neighbor CPU interference.
If NVMe direct-restore driver becomes available in later cycles we can move to hostless rehydrate to reduce PCIe hops.
